title: The Map Is Not the Territory
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay criticizes leaders who communicate strategy by simply handing team members the same dense, jargon-laden document they used to develop it themselves. It argues most team members don't need the full analytical territory — they need a simple map: the big picture, the initiatives involved, and what it means for them personally. The piece proposes a concrete constraint (if a strategic message takes more than ten minutes or five slides, it's probably missing the mark) and uses the map-versus-territory metaphor to argue leaders should hand people direction for action, not a comprehensive description, closing with the reminder that every good map starts with 'You are here.'
points: Criticizes the common practice of communicating strategy by sharing the same dense planning document used to build it, rather than translating it for the audience.
Argues most team members need a simple, actionable map — big picture, initiatives, personal relevance — not the full analytical territory.
Proposes a concrete constraint: if a strategic message takes more than ten minutes or five slides, it's likely missing the mark.
Uses the map-versus-territory metaphor to argue communication should be built for the team, not for other leaders who validate the underlying analysis.
Closes with the reminder that effective strategic communication, like a good map, starts by orienting people to exactly where they stand right now.
quotes: The problem is not the strategy. The strategic plan requires in-depth analysis and a plethora of details to support its soundness. But only the most senior leaders need to know and understand the strategy at that level.
What team members want is a simple explanation of the big picture, the initiatives involved in execution, and what it means for them. Everything else is just noise.
A good rule of thumb is that if it takes more than 10 minutes or five slides to convey, it is probably missing the mark.
Without realizing it, leaders too often design their communication for other leaders, and not for the team members who they want to embrace the strategy.

The best leaders give people a map after they have walked the territory and decided where they want to go. With a great map, team members are instantly primed for action. Like all good maps, they start with “You are here.
